record.original_question: In parallel exact string matching, let p denote the number of processors, t the running time, and n the input length, so that an algorithm is called optimal when pt = O(n). A WRAM is a shared-memory collection of RAMs that allows simultaneous reads and writes with a conflict-resolution mechanism, while a PRAM allows simultaneous reads but not simultaneous writes. Is it possible to design optimal parallel string-matching algorithms for larger processor counts than were then known, for example up to p ≤ n on the WRAM or p ≤ n / log n on the PRAM?

evidence.quote: Question 3: Parallel algorithms. Recently, optimal parallel algorithms (those with pt = O(n), where p = number of processors, t = time) were developed for string matching for a wide range of values of p: on the WRAM for p ≤ n / log n and on the PRAM (for p ≤ n / log² n) ... Is it possible to design optimal parallel algorithms with a larger number of processors (e.g. p ≤ n on the WRAM, p ≤ n/ log n on the PRAM)?

Recall that a WRAM [PRAM] is a collection of RAM's that share a common memory and are allowed simultaneous reads and writes [only simultaneous reads]. In the case of WRAM's, there is in addition a mechanism for resolving write conflicts.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the exact string-matching problem: given a text of length n and a pattern over some alphabet, find all occurrences of the pattern in the text.

A WRAM (concurrent-read concurrent-write parallel random-access machine) is a collection of RAM processors sharing a common memory in which simultaneous reads and simultaneous writes to the same location are permitted, together with a conflict-resolution rule for concurrent writes. A PRAM (concurrent-read exclusive-write parallel random-access machine) is the same model but only simultaneous reads are allowed; concurrent writes are forbidden.

For a parallel algorithm using p processors and running in time t on inputs of length n, call the algorithm optimal if p·t = O(n).

Question: Does there exist an optimal parallel exact string-matching algorithm
(a) on the WRAM that uses up to p ≤ n processors, and
(b) on the PRAM that uses up to p ≤ n / log n processors?

Equivalently, can one design optimal parallel string-matching algorithms running in time t = O(1) on the WRAM and t = O(log n) on the PRAM?
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work resolved the question. Breslauer and Galil gave an optimal O(log log n)-time CRCW-PRAM (WRAM) algorithm using n/log log n processors, and later constant-time optimal parallel string-matching algorithms on the CRCW-PRAM were obtained (Galil, 1995), achieving pt = O(n) with p = n on the WRAM. The matching Ω(log log n) lower bound was also established. On the EREW PRAM, optimal algorithms running in O(log n) time with n/log n processors are known. Thus the targets stated in the question have been achieved.

status_evidence.title: A constant-time optimal parallel string-matching algorithm
status_evidence.snippet: Constant-time optimal parallel string-matching algorithm on the CRCW-PRAM.
status_evidence.claim: An optimal parallel string-matching algorithm exists with p = n processors and t = O(1) on the WRAM/CRCW-PRAM.

status_evidence.title: An Optimal O(log log n) Time Parallel String Matching Algorithm
status_evidence.snippet: O(log log n)-time optimal CRCW-PRAM string matching using n/log log n processors.
status_evidence.claim: Optimal CRCW-PRAM string matching achieves pt = O(n) with t = O(log log n), beating the earlier p ≤ n/log n range.

status_evidence.title: Parallel String Matching (survey chapter)
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys optimal parallel string matching results on PRAM/CRCW models.
status_evidence.claim: Optimal speedup parallel string matching results are now standard textbook material.
